cost statements but close all three realizations as speedups. In particular,
many square dependencies can have entirely trivial productive image. This
wave investigates an explicit change to the generation interface, not a new
name for the unproved character-independence condition.

## Objective and inherited boundary

Find a uniform classical N-only algorithm with lower complete factoring cost.
Keep rigorous complete-factorization bounds, conditional/heuristic NFS costs,
deterministic power bounds and special families distinct. A target here is
to retain subexponential relation costs while establishing useful-root
probability for the actual generation law. A rigorous L_N[1/3,O(1)] complete
algorithm would be a different achievement from improving heuristic GNFS's
constant. Neither is predicted or assumed.

Read AGENTS.md, README.md, docs/SPECIFICATION.md, RESEARCH_LOOP.md,
RESEARCH_TEAM.md, current STATE and W001 synthesis. Also read the W002 B/C
dispositions, H027's corrected section on root fibers and its disposition,
H027-root-entropy-prior-art.md, H028/H031 dispositions, and relevant original
reports for any dependency actually used. Do not rely on old provisional
labels or stale historical lifecycle text over the current dispositions.

H027 already states a sufficient root-fiber condition. Lee–Venkatesan already
identify the productive-character gap, including multiple polynomials. Rabin's
root-inversion reduction and Dixon's uniform-square method are prior art.
Restating those reductions, granting a square-root oracle, or assuming an
odd target is attainable does not satisfy this brief. Current primary leads:

- https://arxiv.org/html/1805.08873v1 (Theorems 2.1/2.3 and section 7).
- https://dspace.mit.edu/entities/publication/15016449-ca26-4d45-82ea-7c200d82d777
  (Rabin, MIT-LCS-TR-212; coordinator checked repository metadata only).
- H027-adaptive-source-dixon-1981.pdf and its source ledger.
- H028/H031's archived Coppersmith and field-square-root sources.

Each child has exclusive outputs, no sibling-draft reads and no recursive
delegation. Parent owns shared state, code and acceptance. This wave allows
symbolic derivation and primary-source inspection/archiving only: no numerical
experiment, example search, benchmark, solver implementation, Lean action,
package install, outside-project write, commit, publication or scheduler.
If a finite test becomes essential, propose one separately with frozen inputs,
seeds, full budgets and a rejection criterion before later authorization.

## Concrete interface to investigate, not a supplied oracle

After paid elementary cases, sample an n-bit word x. Charge rejects x>=N;
inspect gcd(x,N), returning a verified proper factor when possible and counting
full-gcd failures. On a unit branch form R=x^2 mod N. A proposed inner
construction receives only N, R and fresh independent randomness, never x
or any data depending on x beyond R. Selection, stopping and all failures must
respect this restriction. The outer routine may retain x for final recovery.

The known root-inversion reduction suggests an exact conditional useful-root
law if this inner construction outputs a verified y with y^2=R modulo N.
Check its domains, finite-tape law, factor multiplicities and rejected words.
This law alone is not the proposed advance. The hard task is constructing y
with paid generation, reconstruction and a proved adequate probability of
completion. A successful inner law may depend on R but cannot silently
condition on which preimage x was sampled. No known-factor input is allowed.

One possible relation interface is v_j=R^epsilon_j m_j^2 modulo N with
epsilon_j in {0,1}, signed integer v_j and verified unit m_j, all constructed
without x. An integer-square product with odd total epsilon would give a
root of R after paid reconstruction. A zero/nonunit multiplier needs its own
factor-or-failure handling. An even dependency does not supply the desired
odd target merely because the ordinary square kernel is large. Price the
algorithm finding that target; a full square-class oracle is not available.

## Lens A — mixed square-class targets in two number fields

Exclusive report: research/findings/W003-twisted-fields.md.
Exclusive supporting prefix: W003-twisted-*.

Investigate this specific attempted realization. Construct two irreducible
integer polynomials f_1,f_2 from N,R with f_i(R)=0 modulo N, and fields
K_i=Q(alpha_i). The selection rule, coefficient heights, degrees and all
rejections must be explicit and paid. Do not import a small common root or
NFS polynomial-selection law that the actual R distribution does not have.

For common integer pairs (a_j,b_j), the elements a_j^2-b_j^2 alpha_i map
to the same residue a_j^2-b_j^2 R. For a selected subset let
Q(T)=product_j(a_j^2-b_j^2 T). The proposed mixed target is

    Q(alpha_1)=alpha_1 * z_1^2,    Q(alpha_2)=z_2^2,

with actual field roots and valid reductions of z_i. If their reduced images
are units, their ratio is a candidate root of R. This sketch does not assert
that such a subset exists, is cheaply found, or has low norms. Derive the
recovery carefully, with denominator-cleared maps, zero/nonunit images,
reducible polynomials, field embeddings and the opposite target orientation.

Develop one finite algorithm that tries this mixed target. Explain what
information lets its matrix or other search find an inhomogeneous square-class
condition, including units and ideal-class obstructions. Actual root tests
are paid; parity of ideal exponents alone is insufficient. If a square-class
basis or exhaustive subset search is necessary, expose that cost rather than
granting it. Determine whether sign-paired generation forces the target to
be trivial or unattainable, and whether using arbitrary roots R destroys the
usual small-norm geometry. Charge the complete cold trial and restart law.

Compare with existing two-field NFS and modular-square-root methods before
any novelty claim. Seek an actual cost/success improvement; if this specific
realization fails, identify its first concrete obstruction without claiming
all such root-independent constructions impossible. No larger H031 rotation
scan or repetition of its conditional character model is requested.

modular root inversion by relation methods, target square classes, two-field
NFS, quadratic extensions/involutions and rational norm compression. Do not
read Lens A's draft. Determine which parts of the mixed-target sketch are
already existing algorithms and what their complete costs and success
premises actually prove. Inspect primary theorem statements and relevant
algorithms, not only abstracts or search snippets; record retrieval failures.

homogeneous square-kernel availability from an inhomogeneous target, and a
root-fiber reduction from proof that a modified NFS generator retains the
original relation-supply theorem. An exact distributional coupling needs
proof. Check whether known algorithms already realize this interface, even
at a worse bound; do not manufacture novelty from different terminology.

research question. Any new deductions remain unaccepted pending review.
Do not turn a missing theorem in the bounded search into a lower bound or
a claim that no relevant literature exists.

## 2. A finite N-only program and explicit field selection

For complete factorization, first handle 1, use deterministic polynomial-time
primality testing, remove powers of 2, and test perfect powers by exact integer
root searches for exponents `2,...,bit_length(N)`. A discovered `N=M^k` is
handled by recursively factoring M and restoring multiplicities. These are
paid polynomial-bit operations. Every proper factor is checked by division.
Thereafter N is odd, composite and not a perfect power, so it has at least two
distinct prime divisors; repeated prime factors are still allowed.

Put `n=bit_length(N)`. A cold trial draws exactly n independent fair bits as
the integer x. If `x>=N`, return FAIL; this rejection consumes a trial. For
`x<N`, inspect `gcd(x,N)`: return a verified proper factor, count `gcd=N` as
FAIL, and on the unit branch compute `R=x^2 mod N` in `[1,N-1]`. The outer
routine retains x. The inner routine receives only N and R. It is deterministic
here, so its independent-random-tape length is zero. All of its selection,
ordering, root choices, failure and stopping rules depend only on these inputs.

Define

    u = R+2N,
    D_1 = u^2+N,       D_2 = u^2+3N,
    f_i(T) = T^2-D_i,  K_i = Q[T]/(f_i),  alpha_i = T mod f_i.       (2.1)

This is one explicit quadratic-lift rule; it is not a claim of optimal
polynomial selection. The padding makes its termination and irreducibility
independent of any distribution of R.

For both i, `u^2<D_i<(u+1)^2`, since `3N<2u+1`. Thus both polynomials are
irreducible over Q. For `s=u^2+2N`,

    D_1 D_2 = s^2-N^2,
    (s-1)^2 < D_1 D_2 < s^2,                         (2.2)

where the first strict inequality follows from `N^2<2s-1`. Consequently
`D_1 D_2` is not a square. Two nonsquare positive integers define the same
quadratic field only if their product is a rational square, which, for an
integer, would be an integer square. The fields are therefore distinct, not
merely two defining polynomials for one field.

The degree is exactly two, and `4N^2<D_i<10N^2` for odd `N>=3`. Coefficient
bit lengths are `O(n)`. Moreover,

    D_i = R^2 mod N,   f_i(R)=0 mod N,
    gcd(D_i,N)=1,      gcd(f_i'(R),N)=gcd(2R,N)=1.      (2.3)

There is no polynomial-selection rejection loop. As executable validation,
perform integer square tests on `D_1,D_2,D_1D_2`, and check the displayed
congruences and gcds in this order. The proofs show that all pass on the
unit domain. This costs polynomial time and space. No factoring of D_i,
field discriminant, maximal order, or known divisor of N is supplied.

Irreducibility is important: applying a field-square algorithm in a reducible
quotient would be invalid. Here reducibility never occurs. If a different
selection rule produced a factorization `f=gh`, evaluations at R would need
separate gcd tests: a proper gcd is useful, gcd 1 or N is not. One could not
silently keep such an f as a field or credit every rejection as a factor. That
alternative rule is not part of (2.1).

## 3. Relations, target search and actual quadratic-root routine

The finite attempted pair list is `(a_j,b_j)=(j,1)`, `1<=j<=n`, in increasing
j order. Compute the signed integer `v_j=j^2-R` and `gcd(v_j,N)`. Return the
first verified proper factor. If the gcd is N, verify and return the already
known root `y=j mod N` to the outer routine. This is a root-recognition branch,
not success of the mixed-field target; its two trivial outer signs still fail.
If the gcd is 1, retain the original j and the two elements

    g_ij = j^2-alpha_i,
    phi_i(g_ij) = j^2-R mod N.                         (3.1)

Let h be the retained count. On an early-return prefix `0<=h<=n`; reaching
subset search means `h=n`. Nonzero field elements are automatic:
alpha_i is irrational. All retained modular images are units. Thus a product
of retained images is a unit, including the empty product. There is no
smoothness rejection and no claim that a smooth factor base has been built.
This intentionally elementary realization exposes the exact target-search
cost instead of granting a square-class basis.

Enumerate every h-bit subset mask in binary order, including zero. For each
mask recompute, by a sequential scan of retained rows, the two exact products

    Q_i = product_(selected j) (j^2-alpha_i)
        = A_i+B_i alpha_i,   A_i,B_i in Z.             (3.2)

Try the original orientation first. Test `U_1=alpha_1 Q_1` for being a square
in K_1. A root w_1 would give `z_1=w_1/alpha_1` and hence
`Q_1=alpha_1 z_1^2`. Only after this test succeeds, test `U_2=Q_2`, obtaining
`z_2=w_2`. Verify both exact identities and perform §4 recovery. If an actual
root test fails, or recovery cannot yield a valid output, continue to the
opposite orientation: test `alpha_2 Q_2` first and then `Q_1`. After both
orientations fail, advance to the next subset. Return FAIL after exhaustion.

Here is the full terminating square test, with no field-square oracle. In
`K=Q(alpha), alpha^2=D`, where D is a positive nonsquare integer, take
`U=A+B alpha` with integer A,B. A root `w=a+b alpha` must satisfy

    a^2+D b^2=A,       2ab=B.                         (3.3)

If `B=0`, test whether A is a nonnegative rational square and whether A/D is
a nonnegative rational square. The corresponding possible roots are a and
`b alpha`; verify them and choose the first in that order with nonnegative
nonzero coefficient. Zero has its usual unique zero root. If `B!=0`, compute
`E=A^2-D B^2`. A root requires E to be the square of a rational number, hence
of an integer. If E is negative or not an integer square, return NONSQUARE.
For `s=isqrt(E)`, try `t=(A+s)/2` and then `t=(A-s)/2`. For each t which is
a positive rational square, take the positive rational `a=sqrt(t)`, put
`b=B/(2a)`, and verify (3.3). Return the first verified root, or NONSQUARE.

Completeness follows from
`(a^2-D b^2)^2=E` and `a^2=(A +/- sqrt(E))/2`; with `B!=0`, a cannot vanish.
For `B=0`, (3.3) forces `a=0` or `b=0`. A rational-square test reduces its
fraction and tests numerator and denominator by exact integer square roots.
Binary-search integer square roots and schoolbook arithmetic give a
conservative `O((L+log D+1)^3)` bit bound for L-bit input coefficients.
Nonsquare determination is included. The returned root is represented by two
reduced rational numbers and checked exactly, with polynomial bit lengths.

The field roots, if any, are determined without x. No numerical real-root
approximation, external factorization primitive or unbounded enumeration of
possible roots occurs. The only exponential search is the explicitly paid
subset enumeration.

## 4. Denominator-cleared maps and recovery in both orientations

Let `A_i^ord=Z[alpha_i]`, `delta_i=f_i'(alpha_i)=2alpha_i`. Evaluation at R
is a map on this order and extends to

    A_i^ord[alpha_i^(-1),delta_i^(-1)] --> Z/NZ,        (4.1)

because both R and 2R are verified units. There is no map from all of K_i
to Z/NZ. In particular a rational coordinate denominator must not simply be
inverted modulo N.

If `w_i^2=U_i` with the integral U_i used in §3, w_i is an algebraic integer.
The usual order-multiplier fact `f_i'(alpha_i) O_(K_i) subset Z[alpha_i]`
therefore gives

    h_i=delta_i w_i in Z[alpha_i],
    h_i^2=delta_i^2 U_i.                              (4.2)

Compute h_i using exact field arithmetic, cancel rational coordinates, check
that its coefficients are integers, and verify (4.2) before reducing. This
is the same justified order multiplier used in ordinary NFS; the integrality
and invertibility conditions are part of the procedure, not free assumptions.
Stevenhagen §7 describes this multiplier; H031's corrected localization scope
is respected.

On a twisted side, `z_i=w_i/alpha_i`, so define

    zbar_i = h_i(R)/(2R^2) mod N.

On an untwisted side, `z_i=w_i`, so define

    zbar_i = h_i(R)/(2R) mod N.                        (4.3)

Both denominators are verified units. Check the reduced square equations and
gcds. A proper gcd of an image would be a verified factor; a full gcd is a
failure, never a factor. In fact on this retained-row domain all the reduced
roots must be units: their squares, times the unit R where appropriate, equal
the unit `q=Q(R)`. Thus no additional zero or nonunit success is hidden here.

For the original orientation, `R zbar_1^2=zbar_2^2=q`, and the root of R is

    y=zbar_2/zbar_1 mod N.                            (4.4)

For the opposite orientation, `zbar_1^2=R zbar_2^2=q`, and

    y=zbar_1/zbar_2 mod N.                            (4.5)

Verify `y^2=R mod N` before returning y. The outer routine computes both
`gcd(x-y,N)` and `gcd(x+y,N)`, returning only a verified proper divisor.
Changing either field-root sign changes y only by a global sign. Field
embeddings are not new random CRT signs: alpha_i is the fixed algebraic
generator with reduction R; its real embeddings are used to test feasibility,
not interchanged with the reduction map.

## 5. Decisive obstruction: the inhomogeneous target is outside the image

For any field K containing alpha and a real embedding sigma with
`sigma(alpha)<0`, every nonzero pair of rational a,b satisfies

    sigma(a^2-b^2 alpha)=a^2+b^2 |sigma(alpha)|>0.      (5.1)

All products of such elements are positive at sigma. Nonzero squares are
positive there as well. Hence

    product_j (a_j^2-b_j^2 alpha) = alpha z^2          (5.2)

is impossible. z cannot be zero because the product is nonzero. The same
argument allows repeated factors, arbitrary signed a,b, rational a,b, and
negative integer exponents: inverses of positive numbers remain positive.

Both fields (2.1) have the embedding `sigma_i^-(alpha_i)=-sqrt(D_i)`. Thus the
twisted root call in **either** orientation fails on **every** subset. The
mixed-target root completion probability is exactly zero for every admissible
N,R, independently of the row cap. The early recognizable-root branch of §3
remains separate. This is an arithmetic impossibility for
this realization, not just an absent theorem or a conjectured low probability.

More explicitly, the finite-list square-class map would be

    Phi: F_2^h --> (K_1^*/K_1^*2) x (K_2^*/K_2^*2),
    e_j |--> ([g_1j],[g_2j]).                         (5.3)

The targets are `([alpha_1],[1])` and `([1],[alpha_2])`. Real sign is a
well-defined square-class character. At the negative embedding of a twisted
field every column has sign bit 0 and its target has bit 1: the required
linear system includes `0=1`. This single explicit character certifies that
the target is outside the image. No basis for the whole square-class group
is constructed or needed for this negative certificate.

Finite-prime ideal-exponent parities alone would miss that certificate.
Even after those parities vanish, the square-root ideal need not be principal,
and a generator can differ by a nonsquare unit. Nonmaximal-order coordinates
add further complications. Actual tests in §3 decide the element square
condition including all these issues; no class-group or unit oracle is
assumed. Adding the real-sign row rejects this instance before all that work.
The size of a homogeneous kernel says nothing about this inconsistent
inhomogeneous target.

The norm interpretation gives the same obstruction: `a^2-b^2 alpha` is the
relative norm of `a+b sqrt(alpha)` from `K(sqrt(alpha))`. At a negative real
place the extension becomes complex and its nonzero norms are positive.
The target alpha is negative there and cannot be such a norm. This uses only
the displayed elementary real-place identity, not a granted norm solver.

Even adjoining common nonzero rational scalar factors to the two-field rows
does not fix the simultaneous target here: their signs at the two negative
embeddings agree, whereas a mixed target has opposite signs there. Allowing
unpaired elements, different field elements or fields where alpha has no
negative real conjugate changes the interface. This proof does **not** rule
out those choices or claim that sign pairing always forces trivial roots in
every number field.

## 6. Norm geometry and why ordinary NFS supply does not transfer

For arbitrary integers a,b in these quadratic fields,

    Norm_(K_i/Q)(a^2-b^2 alpha_i)=a^4-D_i b^4.         (6.1)

For the actual list `(j,1)`, `1<=j<=n`, and sufficiently large N, `j^4=o(N^2)`
uniformly, so `|j^4-D_i|=Theta(N^2)`. These are actual norm sizes, not just an
upper envelope. For a general box `|a|,|b|<=H`, the simple bound is
`|Norm|<=(1+D_i)H^4`. Cancellation near `a/b=D_i^(1/4)` could give smaller
values, but this trial does not obtain or credit them, and the sign obstruction
would persist even if such values were supplied.

Our arbitrary R is uniform on unit squares only after the outer unit
conditioning; it is not a chosen small NFS common root. The safe lift (2.1)
has height `Theta(N^2)` even for small R. This deliberately paid height gives
no coupling with the usual carefully selected NFS polynomial/root law. The
norm calculation closes the claimed small-norm geometry for **this** selector;
it is not a proof that every N,R-dependent selector needs large coefficients.
Nor does large norm by itself prove a small smoothness probability for a
structured sequence. No such probabilistic substitution is made here.

## 7. Complete trial work, space and success, including early gcds

Write P(n) for a fixed polynomial bound covering the chosen elementary
preprocessing. A scan multiplying (3.2) by `j^2-alpha_i` uses

    A' = j^2 A-D_i B,       B' = j^2 B-A.

Coefficient magnitude grows by at most `D_i+n^2+1` per included row. Thus
products and twisted inputs have coefficient bit length `O((h+1)n)`, at most
`O(n^2)`. Rational roots, order multipliers, exact verification and modular
evaluation all have polynomial bit lengths and costs. Sequential scans and
rewinds suffice; the subset counter has h bits. No large uncharged lookup
table, random-access oracle, square-class advice or amortized field factory
is present.

Selection/validation and all n relation gcd attempts cost polynomial time.
Recomputing a product and applying the explicit root test and possible
reconstruction for one orientation costs conservatively
`O((h+1)^3 n^3)`. There are at most `2^(h+1)` orientations. Hence the literal
finite program has

    T_trial <= P(n)+O(2^h (h+1)^3 n^3) <= 2^n poly(n),
    S_trial <= poly(n).                               (7.1)

Early returns do not pay unexecuted later work. Rejected words, full gcds and
their directly recognized root outputs, all failed subsets, exact nonsquare
tests, integer/rational operand widths
and output verification are included. Space reuses the same product and root
tapes; exponentially many masks are not retained. These are on-paper bit
bounds, not timings.

Let `U_N` be the set of unit residues x for which the ordered inner scan
returns a proper factor before any full-gcd root return. Let `J_N` be the set
of unit-square residues R for which that scan instead returns a directly
recognized root j. These are accounting sets, not supplied to the program;
`|J_N|<=n`. Write r for the number of distinct prime factors of N. The exact
one-word success probability on the continuing domain is

    sigma_N = [N-1-phi(N)+|U_N|+(2^r-2)|J_N|]/2^n.   (7.2)

There are `N-1-phi(N)` proper nonunit words, x=0 is the unique full outer gcd,
and `2^n-N` words are rejected before a gcd. Each R in J_N has `2^r` preimages;
exactly two fail the comparison with its returned j, as proved in §8. The
remaining unit words either give the direct proper gcd in U_N or fail. The
mixed-field root-completion term is zero by §5. Field-selection failures have
mass zero by §2. Formula (7.2) is not being offered as a substitute for a
useful-mass proof.

There is an exact evaluation on distinct semiprimes `N=pq` with `p,q>2n`.
For a unit x, the local sets `x=+/-j mod p` and `x=+/-j mod q` have 2n
distinct members on each side. Neither component in its set means failure.
If both components correspond to the **same** j, the inner scan returns j:
the two equal sign choices fail, and the two opposite sign choices split N.
CRT gives

    unit failures = (p-1-2n)(q-1-2n)+2n,
    sigma_N = (2n+1)(p+q-2-2n)/2^n.                 (7.3)

Different local j indices yield a proper gcd, including when an earlier row
has already returned. Both signs at both primes give 4n recognized-root
preimages, of which 2n succeed and 2n fail.
This is a symbolic count, not a tested example or an independence heuristic.
For balanced p,q tending to infinity it gives `sigma_N=Theta(n/sqrt(N))`.

With probability `(p-1-2n)(q-1-2n)/2^n`, bounded below by a positive constant
for large balanced semiprimes, all n rows are retained and no early factor
occurs. The literal program then makes `2^(n+1)` failed twisted-root calls.
Consequently its expected trial cost is `Omega(2^n)=Omega(N)`. Combining this
with (7.1), (7.3) and iid cold restarts gives expected split cost

    Omega(N^(3/2)/n) <= E T_split <= N^(3/2) poly(n)   (7.4)

on that family. The exponential factor in (7.1) is an actual cost of this
enumeration, not a lower bound on target search generally.

For any continuing composite N, let p be its smallest prime divisor. There
are `N/p-1` nonzero multiples of p below N, each with a proper gcd. Since
`p<=sqrt(N)` and `2^n<=2N`, this already gives `sigma_N=Omega(N^(-1/2))`.
Thus the literal program has the uninteresting general expected split bound

There is an immediate sound optimization with the **same** success law:

## 8. Known root-fiber law checked at the actual interface

This section is a background audit, not the result. Write an odd continuing
N as `product_(i=1)^r p_i^e_i`. Squaring on its unit group has kernel of size
`2^r`: modulo each odd prime power, a root of unity is exactly +1 or -1.
Therefore each unit-square R has exactly `2^r` unit preimages in `[0,N-1]`.
The raw-word law gives each such preimage the same probability `2^(-n)`.

Fix R and any inner transcript, completion event and verified returned y
which depend only on N,R and independent fresh bits. Conditional on these,
x remains uniform on that fiber. Exactly two preimages are `x=+/-y mod N`.
Every other preimage gives a mixed sign across prime powers, and a proper
gcd. The useful probability is exactly `1-2^(1-r)`. Repeated prime factors
do not alter this count; a mixed gcd collects whole prime-power components.
Prime powers have r=1 and zero useful mass, which is why they were handled
by the paid preliminary branch. Even moduli were also handled first.

For a general finite independent inner tape, let a_R be its probability of
returning a proper factor and b_R its disjoint probability of returning a
verified unit root. The failure-inclusive one-word law would be

    (N-1-phi(N))/2^n
      + (2^r/2^n) sum_(R in unit squares)
            [a_R+b_R(1-2^(1-r))].                    (8.1)

Fresh randomness, acceptance and stopping restrictions are essential here.
Our actual routine has `b_R=1` exactly on J_N, from direct root recognition;
the contribution from the mixed-field construction is identically zero.
a_R is its ordered proper-gcd indicator. Thus (8.1) specializes to (7.2), not to
a conditional claim of efficient inversion. H027/Dixon already provide the
fiber reasoning, and the Rabin reduction is prior art.

**Rabin 1979, section 4, Theorems 1–2, printed pp.12–14.**
The input to the assumed algorithm is a quadratic residue, not its preimage.
For a product of two distinct odd primes, one root suffices; uniform preimage
sampling gives a useful mismatch with probability 1/2. Theorem 2 permits success

squaring, verification and failed calls. This is a reduction, not a root-generation

[Institutional report PDF](https://dspace.mit.edu/server/api/core/bitstreams/24c62be8-babb-4ae7-8d00-f042f01cafd6/content).

**Dixon 1981, Algorithm A_L and theorem, pp.256–260.**
The theorem uses v=exp(sqrt(2 log N log log N)) and a random list of length
floor(v^2+1). Expected work is O(v^3), or L_N[1/2,3sqrt(2)], in operations
on N-sized integers; failure fraction is O(list_length^(-1/2)), uniformly
on odd integers with at least two distinct prime factors. Polynomial bit
costs preserve that L constant. Lemma 2 and p.259 give smooth-square supply
without a random-integer heuristic; Lemma 3 conditions on the entire square
list and counts root fibers. Multiplicities are allowed. Section 4 below
pays dense storage explicitly rather than borrowing a sparsity estimate.
[Primary paper](https://pages.cs.wisc.edu/~cs812-1/dixon.pdf).

**Lenstra–Pomerance 1992, main theorem, p.483.**
Their probabilistic algorithm completely factors every positive integer in
expected L_N[1/2,1] time. Internally factoring N, then extracting roots modulo
the obtained prime powers and applying CRT, meets the N,R-only interface with
polynomial expected additional work. It uses no supplied factors. This is an
existing, better rigorous comparison than the conservative Dixon adaptation.
No improved space theorem is inferred from the inspected opening: working
space is bounded by elapsed bit work, and a time-capped invocation also caps
space. Only the main theorem and introductory algorithm description were
inspected here, not its entire proof.
[Primary paper](https://math.dartmouth.edu/~carlp/PDF/paper85.pdf).

Theorem 2.1 gives expected L_N[1/3,(64/9)^(1/3)] square-congruence generation.
Theorem 2.3 needs Conjecture 7.82 for useful congruences on distinct Blum

The following is an explicit extension/accounting of known root-fiber algebra,
**UNACCEPTED here pending review**, not a new root algorithm.

After paid handling of even N, primality and perfect powers, suppose
N=product_{i=1}^k p_i^{e_i} is odd with k>=2. This factorization is used only
in the proof. Let G=(Z/NZ)^*, Q=G^2, and rho_k=1-2^(1-k).
Every R in Q has exactly 2^k unit preimages. At each odd prime power the
ratio of two roots is +1 or -1: their difference and sum cannot both be
divisible by p_i because the roots are units. CRT then gives the fiber count.

One outer trial draws exactly n unbiased bits as x. It rejects x>=N; x=0
has full gcd N and is a failure, not a factor. There are phi(N) unit words,
N-phi(N)-1 words with a proper gcd, and 2^n-N out-of-range words. Conditional
on the unit branch, x is uniform on G and R=x^2 is uniform on Q.

Pad the inner tape to a fixed finite cap. For fixed R and inner tape, all
selection, stopping, field failures and the candidate output are functions
only of N,R and that tape. If the output verifies as y^2=R modulo N, exactly
two of the 2^k possible x are +y or -y. All others make gcd(x-y,N) proper;
it selects a nonempty proper collection of **whole prime-power components**.
Thus, even after conditioning on any successful inner transcript,

    Pr[proper split | verified inner root, unit branch] = rho_k.       (3.1)

The returned y need not itself be uniformly random among roots. It may be
deterministic. What matters is the residual uniformity of x given everything
the inner construction sees. A success probability depending arbitrarily on
R does not change (3.1), since all fibers have the same size. Passing x,
a root-dependent selection bit, or outer gcd-failure feedback to the inner
procedure would invalidate this argument. Fresh outer trials avoid that issue.

For each R, let a_R be the probability that the inner trial returns a verified
proper factor before a root, and s_R the probability that it instead returns
a verified root. These events are disjoint; bad outputs and all cutoffs fail.
The exact success probability per **raw outer word** is

    p_N = (N-phi(N)-1)/2^n
          + phi(N)/2^n * E_{R uniform in Q}[a_R + rho_k s_R].          (3.2)

This includes early factors, full-gcd failure, rejected words, and every inner
failure. For k=1 the root mismatch probability is zero; the elementary
prime-power branch is essential. Even moduli are not covered by this formula.
A Jacobi criterion restricted to Blum semiprimes is unnecessary here.

lifts from p^j to p^(j+1) by solving one linear equation with coefficient
2a modulo p; that coefficient is invertible. Rabin's finite-field root
method, these at-most-n Hensel digits, and CRT require expected poly(n)
additional bit work and polynomial working space. They do not require
supplied factors at the external input.

nodes including multiplicity handling. Uniform monotone L-cost upper envelopes
therefore keep their leading exponent/constant; a Blum-semiprime-only theorem
does not provide this all-input extension.

## 4. A root-independent mixed-integer construction at the old Dixon bound

**On-paper adaptation, UNACCEPTED.** This addresses whether the proposed
interface is already achievable at a worse bound. It does not claim that the
following twist-bit presentation was explicitly published in the inspected
sources. Its supply input is Dixon's proved smooth-square estimate, not a
new assumption or a square-root oracle.

On the continuing domain of section 3, given N and a promised unit square R:

1. Choose an integer B with v<=B<=2v, v=exp(sqrt(2 log N log log N)), for
   N>=3, using certified rounding. Enumerate primes <=B and inspect their
   gcds with N. Return any proper factor. Prime enumeration by elementary
   trial division already costs only O(B^(3/2) poly(n)); no free prime table
   is needed. Let h be the number of primes. After this branch all such
   primes are units and N has no prime divisor <=B.
2. Set T=ceil(16(h+1)B). Use exactly T records of n+1 fresh bits, streamed
   rather than stored: an n-bit word m and an independent bit epsilon.
   Reject m>=N; inspect gcd(m,N), returning proper factors and discarding
   full gcds. On units form v_j=R^epsilon m^2 modulo N in [1,N-1].
   Trial divide v_j by the base, retaining full exponent rows and m,epsilon
   only when completely smooth. Stop at the first h+1 retained rows;
   insufficient rows at the cap give FAIL.
3. Find one nonzero parity dependency c on those rows by deterministic dense
   elimination. Choose it from the v_j/exponent data and record order alone,
   **without using the epsilon labels or m values**. Let E=sum c_j epsilon_j.
   If E is even, return FAIL and restart the entire cold trial independently.
4. If E is odd, compute modulo N

       M = product m_j^c_j,
       S = product_{p<=B} p^(sum_j c_j ord_p(v_j)/2),
       y = S * M^(-1) * R^(-(E-1)/2).                              (4.1)

   All inverses are of verified units. Verify y^2=R and return ROOT(y).
   No huge integer product or hidden factorization is used. Signed integer
   representatives would require a sign row; this construction uses positive
   representatives only.

**Exact coupling.** Fix any h_R in G with h_R^2=R *for the proof only*.
For each accepted residue word define z=h_R^epsilon m modulo N. For each
fixed epsilon, multiplication by h_R^epsilon permutes Z/NZ and preserves
its gcd with N. Hence z is uniform modulo N and independent of epsilon;
v_j=z^2 has exactly Dixon's law. The rejected-word indicator is independent
of epsilon. Conditional on unit admission, smoothness and the whole retained
v_j list, all retained epsilon bits are still independent unbiased bits.
Stopping and the selected nonzero c inspect only that list. Consequently
E is odd with probability exactly 1/2. This is an actual coupling, unlike
an analogy between the shapes of two different NFS relation streams.

For a fixed finite dataset with kappa independent parity dependencies,
the probability that at least one has odd epsilon sum would be
1-2^(-kappa); the displayed algorithm needs only one, so no full square-class
basis is granted. In algebraic terms it seeks a nonzero value of a fresh
random linear functional on a nonzero known kernel. That is the special
reason the inhomogeneous target is available here.

**Supply and probability, with raw rejects included.** Dixon's Lemma 2 and
p.259 show, for sufficiently large N after the small-prime branch, that a
uniform residue z has a positive B-smooth square with probability at least
1/B. Using B>=v only increases smoothness supply. An n-bit raw record
therefore has admission probability at least (N/2^n)/B>1/(2B). In the
hypothetical full T-record tape, the admission count X is binomial with
mean mu>=8(h+1). Chebyshev gives

    Pr[X<h+1] <= mu/(mu-h-1)^2 <= 8/(49(h+1)).                       (4.2)

Early proper gcds only help. Conditional on no such early success and on
completion, the odd-label probability is 1/2 by the coupling. Thus the
probability of FACTOR or ROOT in a capped trial is at least
(1-8/(49(h+1)))/2, in particular greater than 3/8 for sufficiently large N.
No unproved smoothness or field-character independence has been inserted.
For small N the same finite trial has positive completion/root probability
(the residue 1 and its two epsilon realizations suffice), so independent
restarts have finite expectation; a fixed finite initial range may also use
paid exhaustive handling. No uncomputed threshold is an algorithm input.

**Full conservative costs.** There are T=O(B(h+1)) raw attempts, each using
O(h poly(n)) bit work for complete trial division, gcds and residue work.
The retained matrix has h+1 rows of h full exponents and provenance. A
sequential implementation scans each row for every base prime and each pivot
for every elimination pass; dense elimination costs O((h+1)^3 poly(n)).
Record order and provenance eliminate random-access assumptions. Modular
reconstruction, exponent sums, inverses and verification fit that envelope.
All scalar indices have O(n+log B) bits, individual exponents O(log n) bits,
and summed exponents O(log((h+1)n)) bits. Prime-list scans and rejected
records are charged. Therefore

    time per cold capped trial <= B^3 poly(n),
    working space <= B^2 poly(n),
    random tape length <= (n+1)ceil(16(h+1)B).                       (4.3)

The tape is generated online; stopped records can equivalently be padded.
The resulting expected FACTOR-or-ROOT cost is
L_N[1/2,3sqrt(2)] with space L_N[1/2,2sqrt(2)] in this dense realization.
Combining it with section 3 gives the same conservative complete-factoring
L bound: on any unit outer branch, a_R+rho_k s_R is at least half the
inner FACTOR-or-ROOT probability; nonunit outer words add direct success.
Indeed (3.2) is bounded below by
(3/16)(N-1)/2^n for sufficiently large continuing N. Cold restarts thus cost
only a constant factor at each split, and recursion only poly(n).

This is already slower than the rigorous Lenstra–Pomerance complete bound.
If strictly ROOT-only output is required, an inner FACTOR branch can complete
the factor tree by the same verified splitter on smaller factors, then use
prime-power extraction and CRT. Polynomially many recursive subcalls preserve
the stated conservative L bound. This composition supplies no known-factor
input.

It also does not preserve L_N[1/3] relation costs: the uniform residues have
N-sized representatives. Deleting the hidden preimage has not created an
NFS-scale supply theorem. The coupled law concerns **integer residues**;
it supplies no distributional statement for a_j^2-b_j^2 alpha_i.

## 5. The mixed-field target: what is easy, what is being asked

These symbolic checks of the brief are **UNACCEPTED deductions**, independent
of any Lens A draft.

For a finite retained list let q_ij=a_j^2-b_j^2 alpha_i be nonzero and have
common verified unit image v_j. Define the genuine square-class map

    A: F_2^M -> K_1^*/K_1^*2 direct_sum K_2^*/K_2^*2,
    A(c) = ([product q_1j^c_j], [product q_2j^c_j]),
    tau = ([alpha_1],0).                                           (5.1)

The requested subset exists exactly when tau is in im(A). Rank-nullity
establishes something about ker(A), not membership of tau in im(A).
If full square-class coordinates were paid for, this would be an ordinary
inhomogeneous binary solve. Adjoining a target column and finding some
homogeneous dependency is insufficient: its target coefficient must be 1.
If [alpha_1]=0, the target is homogeneous; section 6 handles that separate
square-alpha case. Parity of prime ideals alone omits unit, class-group and
order obstructions.
Random character columns must evaluate the target too and need their own
separation guarantee. They cannot turn an unattainable target into an
attainable one.

For fixed data an entirely finite reference search exists: enumerate all
2^M subsets, multiply their field elements exactly, and factor T^2-alpha_1 Q
and T^2-Q on the two sides. Reject nonsquares, invalid reductions and
nonunits. Use Lenstra's paid algorithm, not a full square-class oracle.
With field degree d, coefficient height H and |a_j|,|b_j|<=A_0, explicit
product widths are polynomial in M,d,log H,log(A_0+1). A conservative envelope
is 2^M (M+1)^3 poly(d,log H,log(A_0+1),n) bit work and polynomial working
space in those parameters, streaming subsets. It decides attainability of
this finite list. If M itself has L_N[1/3,c] size, this fallback is far beyond
an L_N[1/3] algorithm. A better search must be specified and charged.

**Recovery and denominators.** For clarity suppose f_i are monic irreducible
integer polynomials, alpha_i integral, and f_i(R)=0 modulo N. Factorization
and irreducibility checks are paid. If a proposed defining polynomial is
reducible, evaluate its factors at R and inspect proper gcds; reducibility
alone does not promise a split. A full gcd N is not a proper factor.

If Q(alpha_1)=alpha_1 z_1^2 and Q(alpha_2)=z_2^2, instead extract

    w_1^2=alpha_1 Q(alpha_1),      w_2^2=Q(alpha_2).                  (5.2)

Here w_1=alpha_1 z_1; both w_i are integral, avoiding an unjustified claim
that z_1 itself is integral. Let delta_i=f_i'(alpha_i),
D_i=f_i'(R) modulo N. Check gcd(D_i,N): a proper value is a factor;
full gcd fails this localization; only gcd=1 permits inversion.
The order multiplier gives H_i=delta_i w_i in Z[alpha_i]. Compute this in
the exact field, cancel rational output denominators, verify integer
coefficients and H_i^2=delta_i^2 w_i^2, then reduce

    u_i=H_i(R)/D_i modulo N.

The map is on Z[alpha_i,delta_i^(-1)], not all of K_i. Now
u_1^2=R V and u_2^2=V with V=product v_j, so both u_i are units and

    y=u_1/u_2,                 y^2=R modulo N.                     (5.3)

Equivalently the original reduced z_i give y=z_2/z_1. Opposite orientation
Q(alpha_1)=z_1^2, Q(alpha_2)=alpha_2 z_2^2 reverses the roles and yields
u_2/u_1. Verify the final congruence. Different field-root signs merely
negate y and leave (3.1) unchanged.

For nonmonic f with leading coefficient l, one may use the integral generator
theta=l alpha and monic F(T)=l^(d-1)f(T/l), with theta mapping to lR.
All l inversions and derivative denominators need unit checks, coefficient
height conversion, and paid exact arithmetic. A leading coefficient with
proper gcd gives a factor; full gcd can obstruct this implementation.
Zero q_ij or zero images are outside the square-class domain: inspect gcds
and either output a proper factor or reject. No universal fraction-field map
or discriminant inverse is granted.

## 6. Quadratic extensions, involutions, and rational norm compression

Assume alpha is nonzero and nonsquare in K, and set
L=K(beta), beta^2=alpha, tau(beta)=-beta. Then

    a^2-b^2 alpha = Norm_{L/K}(a-b beta).                           (6.1)

This is ordinary quadratic norm algebra. It does **not** map beta to a known
residue modulo N: evaluating beta would already require a root of R.
The coefficient representation of L is computable without such an evaluation.
If alpha is square in K, the algebra splits instead of defining a quadratic
field; test this separately. In that case a valid reduction of its field
root already gives a root of R, with the same paid denominator checks.

**A necessary norm condition for the twisted side.** Every product Q of
(6.1) is a norm. Every z^2 with z in K is also a norm. Consequently

    Q=alpha z^2  implies alpha in Norm_{L/K}(L^*).

Since Norm(beta)=-alpha, this is equivalent to

    -1 in Norm_{L/K}(L^*).                                        (6.2)

Condition (6.2) is necessary, not sufficient for the finite retained subset
problem: even the entire norm group is larger than the generated list.
No free norm-equation solver or class-group computation is inferred.

A concrete obstruction needs no numerical test. If K has a real embedding
sigma with sigma(alpha)<0, every retained nonzero a^2-b^2 alpha is strictly
positive under sigma, while sigma(alpha z^2)<0 for nonzero z. Thus the
twisted target is unattainable for **every** such product in that field.
It is also the familiar local obstruction to -1 being a norm from a complex
quadratic extension at that real place. Positive-at-all-real-places alpha
avoids this particular obstruction; it does not prove attainability.
For the opposite target orientation, apply the test to the other field.

**Why a homogeneous extension trick can erase the target.** If an algorithm
makes A(beta)=product(a_j-b_j beta) an actual square in L, then
A(beta)A(-beta)=Norm(A) is a square in K. That method selects the untwisted
class automatically. It cannot give nontrivial [alpha] by merely pairing the
same square dependency with its conjugate.

There is a weaker condition that retains both possibilities:

    Q in K^* intersect L^*2  iff  Q in K^*2 or Q in alpha K^*2.       (6.3)

Indeed if (u+v beta)^2 is in K, its beta coefficient 2uv is zero, so its
root lies either in K or beta K. Equivalently tau(w)=+w or -w for a square
root w of Q in L. A homogeneous square condition in L therefore needs an
additional invariant/anti-invariant choice to select the mixed target in
the two fields. The extra bit has no proved balanced distribution here.
Taking rational norms does not recover that lost bit.

For monic f of degree d,

    Norm_{K/Q}(a^2-b^2 alpha)
       = sum_{r=0}^d f_r a^(2r) b^(2d-2r),
    |Norm| <= (d+1)H max(|a|,|b|)^(2d).                            (6.4)

The formula is valid also at b=0 by homogenization. It is a size upper
bound, not a smoothness or small-value theorem. Norm functoriality makes
rational norm compression an arithmetic identity, not a free increase in
usable relations. Full norms aggregate primes over distinct ideals and lose
square-class information; a rational square norm is not a certificate of a
field square. The legitimate automorphism methods in section 2 keep
additional arithmetic structure and have explicit input premises.

## 7. Why the NFS supply theorem has not transferred

This is a comparison of the frozen brief to the inspected algorithms, not a
claim about what Lens A ultimately submitted.

The changed input root is R, uniform in Q on the outer unit branch. It is not
LV's selected m near N^(1/d), and the generator a^2-b^2 alpha restricts the
linear coefficients to squares. Correlations between both fields, common
pairs, retained lists and target labels must be proved for their actual law.
Random polynomial perturbation at R alone does not show that their joint
norms have LV's distribution.

For example, for any prescribed numerical cutoff U,

    Pr[R<=U | outer unit] <= (floor(U)+1) 2^k / phi(N).              (7.1)

On growing balanced distinct semiprimes, a cutoff U=L_N[2/3,c] therefore
captures at most N^(-1+o(1)) of that law. This count rules out casually
identifying the handed-in R with a usual small integer root; it does not
rule out small-height polynomials at other representations of R, paid
lattice selection, or a different successful construction.

There are three separate obligations: obtain useful low-norm relations;
find the prescribed actual square class among them; and extract and reduce
its roots at the advertised full bit cost. Section 3 resolves the *fourth*
step, useful outer mismatch, if all three have succeeded without seeing x.
The known square-congruence theorem resolves neither their modified supply
law nor their target membership. The exact integer coupling in section 4
shows the standard of proof required for any claimed transfer.

## 8. Disposition, unsupported statement, and one next proof

**Disposition:** source/reduction gate delivered; no new complete factoring
improvement and no completed review of Lens A. Known algorithms already
realize root inversion. Two-field NFS, conjugation norms and extraction of
existing field squares are not new ingredients. The randomized integer
adaptation and norm/involution checks above remain UNACCEPTED deductions.

**Unsupported positive statement:** a uniformly specified cold N,R-only
mixed-field construction has a cold mean cost C and an actual completion probability s for which
C/s is L_N[1/3,O(1)], uniformly over the required inputs. Neither the
bounded literature inspection nor this report proves it. In particular there
is no demonstrated inverse-polynomial target-attainment mass, preserved
LV relation law, or improved Coppersmith-matched heuristic constant.
A missing theorem in this search is not a nonexistence or hardness result.

**One next proof that could change the conclusion:** for the eventual frozen
Lens A generator, prove a lower bound on the actual paid probability of
reaching tau in (5.1), after all polynomial, real-place/norm, relation and
root-reduction failures, strong enough that C_N/p_N has the claimed complete
L_N[1/3] envelope. The proof must specify the joint generation law and justify
any coupling it uses. Homogeneous nullity alone fails this criterion.
No finite test or implementation is proposed by this source task.

After elementary cases, assume N is odd, gcd(N,15)=1, and R is a unit
represented by 1<=R<N. A proper gcd with 3 or 5 is an earlier verified factor;
their prime/power cases belong to preprocessing. No hidden root x is passed.

    Tr(w)^2 = Tr(alpha)+2Norm(w) = s+2t or s-2t.
